description: Each component: what it is, the signal in a prompt that says reach for it, what it costs, how it breaks, and every canonical design problem that uses it — with what it is doing there.

components.title: Load Balancer
components.what: A single address in front of many interchangeable servers, spreading requests and routing around dead ones.
reachFor: The prompt says a fleet of stateless app servers behind one endpoint
You need to survive a server dying without the client noticing
Traffic must be added to or removed from a pool during a deploy
avoid: The backends are NOT interchangeable — a request must reach one specific shard owner, which is routing, not balancing
You reach for it to solve a database bottleneck; balancing the tier in front of the bottleneck moves nothing
costs: One more hop of latency and one more thing that can be misconfigured
It becomes the failure domain — an LB outage is a total outage, so it needs its own redundancy
Health-check tuning is a real tradeoff: aggressive checks eject healthy nodes, lax ones send traffic into a black hole
failureModes: Sticky sessions defeat even distribution and turn one hot client into one hot server
A slow-but-alive backend passes health checks while poisoning latency for everyone routed to it
Cascading ejection: checks eject nodes under load, concentrating load on the survivors, which then fail checks too

alternatives.note: DNS steers between REGIONS; an LB steers between servers. Different blast radius, different failover speed.
Discovery lets the caller pick a backend itself, removing the middle hop — normal for internal service-to-service.

components.title: Reverse Proxy
components.what: A server-side intermediary that terminates the client connection and speaks to backends on its behalf, so cross-cutting work happens once at the edge.
reachFor: TLS termination, compression, or request buffering should happen in one place, not in every service
You want to serve static assets and proxy dynamic paths from the same hostname
Slow clients must not tie up application threads
avoid: The only need is spreading load — that is a load balancer, and calling it a proxy adds vocabulary without adding a decision
Per-caller policy, auth and quotas are the real requirement — that is an API gateway
costs: Another network hop and another config surface
Buffering large uploads costs memory at the edge
It sees plaintext after TLS termination, so it becomes a security-relevant component
failureModes: Header and body size limits silently truncate or reject at the edge, producing errors the backend never sees
Connection-pool exhaustion to backends throttles everything behind it
Timeout mismatches between proxy and backend produce duplicated work: the proxy retries a request still running

alternatives.note: A gateway is a reverse proxy that also owns auth, rate limits and per-route policy. Pick it when policy is the point.
If nothing cross-cutting happens at the hop, you only needed balancing.

components.title: API Gateway
components.what: The single front door for external callers: authenticates, applies quota, routes to the right service, and normalises the response.
reachFor: The prompt has many backend services but one public API surface
Auth, rate limiting and request validation must be enforced before traffic reaches any service
Clients need one contract while services behind it change shape
avoid: Internal service-to-service calls — a gateway in the middle of a mesh adds a hop and a bottleneck for no policy benefit
It becomes a place to put business logic; that turns the gateway into an undeployable monolith everyone is afraid of
costs: A shared choke point: its capacity is the API's capacity, and its deploys are everyone's deploys
Latency on every single request, including ones that needed nothing from it
Route config becomes a distributed-ownership problem across teams
failureModes: Auth-service dependency makes the gateway fail closed and take the whole API down with it
Per-route config drift: a service ships a new endpoint the gateway does not know about
Fan-out aggregation inside the gateway turns one client timeout into N abandoned backend calls

alternatives.note: If you need TLS and routing but no per-caller policy, a plain reverse proxy is less machinery.
The gateway is usually WHERE rate limiting lives; the limiter is the mechanism, the gateway is the venue.

components.title: Service Discovery
components.what: A registry that answers 'where is service X right now', so callers reach live instances without hardcoded addresses.
reachFor: Instances come and go constantly — autoscaling, rolling deploys, container schedulers
Internal callers should route directly to backends rather than through a shared LB
The prompt mentions a service mesh or sidecar proxies
avoid: A fixed, small set of long-lived hosts — a config file is honest and has no failure mode
You need routing decisions based on request CONTENT; discovery answers 'where', not 'which one for this request'
costs: A strongly-consistent registry is itself a distributed system to run and to keep available
Client-side libraries must be kept in step across every language you deploy
Registration lag means the registry is always slightly behind reality
failureModes: Stale entries route traffic to instances that are already gone
Registry outage is a total outage unless callers cache last-known-good and fail static
Thundering herd of re-registration after a network partition heals

alternatives.note: A load balancer centralises the same decision; discovery distributes it to callers. One hop vs. one library everywhere.
DNS is discovery with weak TTL semantics — fine for coarse-grained, wrong for second-by-second membership.

components.title: DNS & Anycast Routing
components.what: Steering users to a region or PoP before a connection is ever made, using DNS answers or a single IP announced from many locations.
reachFor: The prompt is global and the first requirement is 'users hit the nearest region'
You need region-level failover, not server-level
Traffic must be split by geography, weight or latency at the entry point
avoid: Fast failover is required — resolver and client TTL caching means DNS changes take minutes to hours to propagate
You are steering individual requests; by the time DNS answered, the request already committed to an address
costs: TTL is a tradeoff you cannot escape: short TTLs cost query volume, long TTLs cost failover time
Clients and resolvers routinely ignore your TTL anyway
Anycast requires network-layer control most teams do not have in-house
failureModes: Stale cached answers keep sending users to a region you just drained
Anycast route flaps mid-connection can break long-lived TCP sessions
GeoDNS resolves by RESOLVER location, not user location — a centralised corporate resolver mis-steers a whole company

alternatives.note: Use DNS to pick the region, an LB to pick the server. They compose; they do not compete.
A CDN already does global steering as part of its product — usually the cheaper answer for static content.

components.title: Cache
components.what: A fast store holding the answer to work you already did, so the expensive path runs once for many reads.
reachFor: The prompt gives a lopsided read:write ratio — 100:1 and up
The answer is expensive to compute or fetch and changes far more slowly than it is read
A stated staleness tolerance ('feed can be up to a minute old') is an explicit invitation
avoid: Reads must reflect writes immediately — a cache is a correctness hazard you added on purpose
The working set is uniformly random over a huge keyspace; the hit rate will not pay for the machinery
Write-heavy workloads where you would spend more invalidating than serving
costs: Every cache is a second copy of the truth, and now you own the invalidation problem
Memory is expensive, so capacity forces an eviction policy you must justify
Debugging gets harder: behaviour now depends on whether something was warm
failureModes: Stampede — a hot key expires and every concurrent request hits the origin at once
Hot key — a single entry exceeds one node's throughput no matter how many nodes you add
Cold start after a flush or deploy sends full production load at a database sized for cache-miss traffic
Silent staleness: an invalidation is missed and wrong data is served indefinitely with no error

alternatives.note: Same idea moved to the network edge. Pick a CDN when the payload is static and the win is geographic distance.
If reads are QUERIES rather than key lookups, a precomputed index beats caching every distinct query.

components.title: CDN
components.what: A globally distributed cache of your static bytes, serving users from a nearby PoP instead of your origin.
reachFor: The payload is large, static and read by many people — images, video segments, JS bundles
The prompt names a global user base and latency is a stated requirement
Origin egress bandwidth is the thing that will not scale
avoid: Responses are personalised per user — you are caching a thing with an audience of one
Content must be revoked instantly; purge propagation is not immediate
The bottleneck is compute, not distance or bandwidth
costs: You now have cache state in hundreds of places you cannot inspect
Purge is eventually consistent and often billed per request
Cache-key design becomes a real engineering problem the moment headers or query strings vary
failureModes: Stale asset served long after deploy because the URL did not change
Cache fragmentation: a varying header splits one hot object into thousands of cold ones
Origin shielding absent, so a cold global cache means every PoP independently stampedes the origin

alternatives.note: An origin-side cache when the win is compute, not distance.
When the response must be assembled per request but you still want it done near the user.

components.title: Hot-Key Mitigation
components.what: Techniques for the one key whose traffic exceeds what a single shard or cache node can serve — replicate it, split it, or absorb it locally.
reachFor: The prompt contains a celebrity, a viral item, or a flash sale on one SKU
Load is skewed enough that adding shards does not help because the skew rides along
One partition is saturated while the rest of the fleet is idle
avoid: Load is genuinely uniform; you are solving a problem the workload does not have
The hot entity needs strong consistency — replicating it multiplies the write-coordination cost
costs: Key splitting (key#1..key#N) pushes fan-in complexity to every reader
Local in-process caches multiply staleness windows by the number of app servers
Detection needs per-key telemetry you probably are not collecting yet
failureModes: Mitigation applied statically, so yesterday's celebrity is replicated and today's is melting a shard
Split counters read before all sub-keys are summed, producing numbers that go backwards
The hot key is a WRITE key, so replication makes contention worse rather than better

alternatives.note: Solves uneven placement, not uneven demand. Virtual nodes will not save you from one viral key.
A local cache tier in front absorbs read skew without touching the sharding scheme.

components.title: Edge Compute
components.what: Running small amounts of your logic in the CDN's PoPs, so personalisation, auth or rewriting happens near the user instead of at origin.
reachFor: Responses need small per-user variation but the bulk is cacheable
A redirect, A/B assignment or token check should not cost a round trip to origin
You want to cache aggressively but the cache key depends on a computed value
avoid: The logic needs your primary database — you have moved the compute but not the data
Anything requiring long execution, large memory, or strong consistency
costs: A constrained runtime with tight CPU and memory limits and a restricted API surface
Deploys now target a fleet you do not operate, with its own rollout semantics
Debugging and observability at the edge is markedly worse than at origin
failureModes: Edge logic diverges from origin logic and the two disagree about the same request
A bad edge deploy has global blast radius and no gradual rollout
Cold starts add latency to exactly the requests you moved to the edge to speed up

alternatives.note: If the variation can be pushed into the URL, plain CDN caching is simpler and faster.
Central policy at origin when consistency of the rule matters more than the round trip.

components.title: Relational Database
components.what: Row storage with a fixed schema, joins, secondary indexes and multi-row ACID transactions.
reachFor: The prompt says money, inventory, bookings, or anything where a partial write is a bug with a lawyer attached
Entities are related and access patterns are not known up front — joins buy you flexibility
You need read-your-writes and cross-row invariants enforced by the store
avoid: Write volume that exceeds one primary and the data has no clean partition key
Schemaless, high-churn documents where every row would be half null
Append-only telemetry at millions of events per second
costs: Vertical scaling has a ceiling and horizontal scaling means sharding you implement yourself
Schema migrations on large tables are an operational event, not a deploy
Joins that were free at 1M rows are a capacity plan at 1B
failureModes: Lock contention on a hot row serialises the whole workload
Connection exhaustion from an app tier that scaled out faster than the pool
An unindexed query pattern discovered in production as a full table scan

alternatives.note: If every access is by primary key and you need no transactions, a KV store scales further for less.
When write volume and partition-key access dominate and you can give up joins.

components.title: Key-Value Store
components.what: A hash table with an operations team: get and put by key, partitioned across nodes, no query language.
reachFor: Every access in the prompt is 'look this up by its id'
You need very high throughput and predictable single-digit-millisecond latency
The value is opaque to the store — a session, a blob of JSON, a serialized object
avoid: You will need to query by anything other than the key; you would be building indexes by hand
Cross-key transactions or invariants
Analytical scans over the whole dataset
costs: Access patterns are frozen into the key design, and changing them means a migration
Secondary indexes, if the store has them, are usually eventually consistent
You own denormalisation and therefore the consistency between copies
failureModes: Hot partition from a key design that concentrates traffic
Unbounded value growth turning one key into a multi-megabyte read
Eventual consistency surfacing as a read that does not contain the write you just made

alternatives.note: The moment two rows must change together, you want transactions more than you want throughput.
Same key-based access but with queryable structure inside the value.

components.title: Document Store
components.what: Key-value where the value is a structured document the engine can index and query inside.
reachFor: Entities are self-contained and read as a whole — a product, a profile, an order with its lines
The schema varies per record or evolves quickly
You want secondary indexes without committing to a rigid schema
avoid: Data is highly relational and the same fact would be duplicated across many documents
You need multi-document transactions as the normal case, not the exception
Aggregations across the entire collection are the primary workload
costs: Denormalisation means one fact lives in many documents and updates fan out
Unbounded arrays inside a document become an anti-pattern that is painful to undo
Schema flexibility becomes schema drift without discipline in the application layer
failureModes: Documents grow past the engine's size limit and writes start failing
Index bloat from indexing fields inside large nested structures
Application-level joins doing N+1 fetches that a relational engine would have planned

alternatives.note: When the same entity is read in many different shapes, normalise and join instead of duplicating.
For full-text or faceted query over documents, a search engine is the right tool.

components.title: Wide-Column Store
components.what: Partition-key-first storage (Cassandra, HBase, DynamoDB) built for enormous write volume and range scans within a partition.
reachFor: Write throughput is the headline requirement and writes are spread across many partition keys
Access is always 'give me a range within one partition' — a user's messages, a device's readings
The prompt needs multi-region writes with tunable consistency
avoid: Query patterns are unknown or will change — the partition key is close to irreversible
You need joins, or transactions spanning partitions
The dataset is small enough that one relational primary would do
costs: You design tables per query, so a new access pattern means a new table and a backfill
Tombstones and compaction are operational concerns that leak into latency
Eventual consistency by default; strong reads cost latency and availability
failureModes: Unbounded partition growth turning one partition into a hotspot and then a timeout
Tombstone accumulation making range scans progressively slower until compaction catches up
Last-write-wins silently discarding a concurrent update

alternatives.note: If every row is a timestamped measurement, a purpose-built TSDB gives you retention and rollups for free.
When you never need range scans within a partition, plain KV is simpler.

components.title: Time-Series Store
components.what: A store specialised for append-only timestamped measurements, with automatic downsampling, retention and time-range queries.
reachFor: The prompt is metrics, telemetry, IoT readings, or click events keyed by time
Old data becomes less valuable at a predictable rate and can be rolled up
Queries are almost always 'this series, this window, this aggregate'
avoid: Records get updated after they are written — TSDBs assume append-only
High-cardinality dimensions per point; label cardinality is the classic way to melt one
You need transactional guarantees or joins
costs: Cardinality is the budget, and it is easy to blow up accidentally
Retention and rollup policy is a product decision you must make early
Another store class to operate and to back up
failureModes: Cardinality explosion from a label like user_id or request_id
Queries spanning long windows at full resolution overwhelming memory
Late-arriving points landing after a window was already rolled up

alternatives.note: If the aggregate matters more than the raw points, compute it in-flight and never store them.
A generic partition-by-entity, cluster-by-time table when you need control over the layout.

components.title: Object / Blob Storage
components.what: Cheap, effectively unbounded storage for immutable files addressed by key, with HTTP access and lifecycle tiering.
reachFor: The prompt has large binary payloads — images, video, backups, documents
The bytes are written once and read many times
Storage cost at scale is a stated concern, or the data must outlive any server
avoid: You need to update a small part of an object; blob stores replace, they do not patch
Access needs to be transactional with your database
Latency requirements are single-digit milliseconds
costs: Eventually-consistent listing and metadata in many implementations
Egress is the line item that surprises people, which is why a CDN sits in front
Two systems now hold related state — the object and the row that describes it
failureModes: Orphaned objects when the database row is deleted but the object is not, or vice versa
Uploads going through the app tier and saturating it, instead of client-direct with presigned URLs
Hot prefixes throttling throughput in stores that partition by key prefix

alternatives.note: For very large or resumable payloads, chunk before you store — it changes the failure story entirely.
Blob storage holds the bytes; a CDN is how users actually get them without paying origin egress.

components.title: Chunking
components.what: Splitting a large payload into independently addressable pieces, so transfer, retry, dedup and parallelism operate per piece.
reachFor: Files are large enough that a failed transfer must not restart from zero
Only part of a file typically changes between versions
You want parallel upload or download, or per-piece deduplication
avoid: Payloads are small; per-chunk metadata will exceed the data
The consumer needs the whole object anyway and cannot start early
costs: A manifest per object, and now the manifest is a consistency problem of its own
Chunk-size choice is a real tradeoff: small chunks dedup better, large chunks cost less metadata
Reassembly and ordering logic on the read path
failureModes: Partial uploads leaving orphan chunks nobody garbage collects
Manifest written before all chunks are durable, producing an object that reads as corrupt
Fixed-size chunking defeating dedup because one inserted byte shifts every boundary

alternatives.note: Multipart upload gives you most of the retry benefit without you owning a manifest.
Chunking is usually the enabler for dedup rather than an end in itself.

components.title: Deduplication
components.what: Storing identical content once by addressing it with a hash of its bytes, so repeats cost a reference instead of a copy.
reachFor: The prompt implies heavy duplication — shared files, re-uploads, mirrored pages
Storage or bandwidth cost is an explicit constraint
You need to detect 'have I already processed this?' cheaply
avoid: Content is unique by nature; you pay hashing cost for nothing
Per-copy metadata or permissions must differ, and a shared object cannot carry them
costs: Hashing on the write path, and a content-address index that must itself scale
Reference counting, which means deletion is now a distributed garbage-collection problem
Cross-tenant dedup raises real security and isolation questions
failureModes: Reference count leaks so nothing is ever reclaimed
Deleting an object still referenced by another user
Hash collision handling ignored entirely because it 'cannot happen'

alternatives.note: If you only need 'have I seen this before' and can tolerate false positives, a bloom filter is far cheaper.
Chunk-level dedup catches partial overlap that whole-file dedup misses.

components.title: Sharding
components.what: Splitting one logical dataset across many machines by a partition key, so capacity and throughput scale horizontally.
reachFor: The dataset or its write volume exceeds what one machine can hold or serve
The prompt gives numbers that clearly exceed one primary
There is a natural partition key with high cardinality and even distribution
avoid: One machine still fits — sharding is a permanent complexity tax paid in advance
Queries routinely span all partitions; you have built scatter-gather, not scale
No good key exists and every candidate is skewed
costs: Cross-shard queries and transactions become application problems
Resharding is a migration with a data-movement plan, not a config change
Every operational task multiplies by the shard count
failureModes: Skew: one partition holds the celebrity and saturates while others idle
Scatter-gather latency governed by the slowest shard, so p99 degrades as shards are added
A key chosen for even distribution that forces every read to fan out

alternatives.note: The placement scheme that makes adding and removing shards cheap; sharding is the what, this is the how.
If reads are the bottleneck and the data fits, replicas scale reads without splitting anything.

components.title: Replication
components.what: Keeping copies of the same data on multiple nodes, for read capacity, fault tolerance, or geographic proximity.
reachFor: Durability or availability is a stated requirement — losing one node must not lose data
Read volume dwarfs write volume and the dataset fits on one machine
Users are geographically spread and reads should be served locally
avoid: Writes are the bottleneck — replication multiplies write work rather than reducing it
The application cannot tolerate reading a value that is momentarily behind
costs: Replication lag is now a semantic your application must handle explicitly
Synchronous replication trades latency and availability for consistency; asynchronous trades the reverse
N× storage and N× write amplification
failureModes: Read-your-writes violated because a read landed on a lagging replica
Split brain during a partition, with two nodes both accepting writes
Failover promoting a replica that had not caught up, silently losing acknowledged writes

alternatives.note: Quorum reads/writes let you tune the consistency-availability point instead of accepting the default.
Replication scales reads; sharding scales writes and capacity. Most real systems need both.

components.title: Consistent Hashing
components.what: Placing keys and nodes on a ring so adding or removing a node moves only ~1/N of keys instead of remapping everything.
reachFor: Membership changes routinely — autoscaling caches, nodes failing and returning
A remap would invalidate a cache wholesale and stampede the origin
You need a placement rule every client can compute without asking a coordinator
avoid: The node set is fixed and rare changes can be handled by a planned migration
Load is skewed by demand rather than by key count — the ring cannot fix a viral key
costs: Virtual nodes are required for even distribution, which means more ring metadata
Every client needs the same ring view, so ring membership becomes shared state
Range queries are impossible; the hash destroys ordering by design
failureModes: Too few virtual nodes producing badly uneven load
Clients disagreeing about ring membership and writing the same key to different nodes
Cascading failure as a dead node's share lands entirely on its ring successor

alternatives.note: Range-based sharding when you need ordered scans and can accept manual rebalancing.
The ring balances key COUNT, never key DEMAND — pair it with hot-key handling.

components.title: Quorum (N/W/R)
components.what: Requiring W acknowledgements to write and R responses to read out of N replicas, tuning consistency against availability.
reachFor: The prompt asks you to reason explicitly about the consistency-availability tradeoff
You want strong reads sometimes and fast reads other times, from the same store
Replicas span regions and you must survive losing one
avoid: A single-leader store already gives you what you need with less to explain
The application cannot handle the conflict resolution that concurrent writes require
costs: Latency is governed by the slowest replica in the quorum
W+R>N gives overlap, not linearizability — concurrent writes still need conflict resolution
Operational reasoning gets harder; correctness now depends on numbers in a config
failureModes: Sloppy quorum accepting writes on nodes outside the intended set, so a later read misses them
Read repair storms after a partition heals
Choosing W+R≤N for latency and quietly accepting stale reads nobody documented

alternatives.note: Plain leader-follower replication when you do not need per-request tuning.
Quorums make concurrent writes possible; something still has to decide who wins.

components.title: Distributed ID Generation
components.what: Producing unique identifiers across many machines without a central allocator — Snowflake-style, UUID, or ranged counters.
reachFor: Many nodes must mint ids concurrently without coordinating on every one
Ids need to be roughly time-ordered for index locality or pagination
The prompt needs short, opaque or non-guessable public identifiers
avoid: One database's auto-increment still keeps up — it is simpler and monotonic
Ids must be strictly gapless or sequential, which distributed generation cannot promise
costs: Snowflake-style ids need a machine-id assignment scheme and clock discipline
Random UUIDs destroy index locality and inflate B-tree page splits
Encoding choices leak information — a sequential id tells competitors your volume
failureModes: Clock skew or NTP step-back producing duplicate or out-of-order ids
Machine-id collision after a scaling event reuses an identifier
Range allocator becoming a single point of failure everyone forgot was in the path

alternatives.note: A single auto-increment column is correct and boring until you actually outgrow one primary.
If the id only needs to route, hashing an existing natural key may remove the problem.

components.title: Work Queue
components.what: A durable buffer of tasks between a producer and a pool of workers, so slow work happens outside the request path.
reachFor: The prompt has work that must happen but not before the user gets a response
Producer and consumer rates differ, especially in bursts
Retries need to be automatic and durable across a worker crash
avoid: The caller needs the result to continue — you have added latency and a callback problem
Strict end-to-end ordering across all work is required
The work is trivial; a queue adds an operational component to save nothing
costs: Eventual consistency becomes visible to users ('it will appear in a moment')
Another durable system to run, monitor and reason about
Every consumer must be idempotent, because delivery is at-least-once
failureModes: Unbounded backlog growth when consumers cannot keep up, turning latency into an outage
Poison message retried forever, blocking the queue behind it
Duplicate processing from redelivery after a consumer crash mid-work

alternatives.note: A queue gives each message to ONE consumer; pub/sub gives it to all of them. Different question.
A queue absorbs bursts; it does not fix a consumer that is permanently too slow.

components.title: Pub/Sub
components.what: One published event delivered to every interested subscriber, so producers never learn who consumes them.
reachFor: Several unrelated systems must react to the same event
You want to add a new consumer later without touching the producer
The prompt describes an event that fans out to notifications, analytics and search indexing at once
avoid: Exactly one worker should handle each item — that is a work queue
The producer needs to know the work completed
costs: No single place shows what happens when an event fires; tracing gets harder
Every subscriber is a new failure mode for the same event
Schema evolution must satisfy consumers you may not know about
failureModes: A slow subscriber applying backpressure to the whole topic, or being silently dropped
Event-schema change breaking a consumer nobody remembered existed
Redelivery producing duplicate side effects in every subscriber at once

alternatives.note: When the work must happen once, not N times.
If the event must be exactly as durable as the database write that caused it.

components.title: Fan-out
components.what: Turning one write into many per-recipient writes — precomputing on write (push) instead of assembling on read (pull).
reachFor: Reads vastly outnumber writes and the read must be fast
The prompt describes feeds, timelines or notifications with a follower graph
The per-recipient view is expensive to assemble at query time
avoid: One writer has millions of recipients — write amplification explodes
Recipients rarely read what you precomputed; you did the work for nothing
The content changes after delivery and every copy would need updating
costs: Storage for N copies of what was logically one item
Write amplification proportional to the fan-out degree
Deletes and edits must chase every copy you created
failureModes: Celebrity write becoming a thundering-herd event that stalls the fan-out pipeline
Partial fan-out on failure leaving some recipients with the item and others without
Unbounded per-recipient lists growing forever because nothing caps them

alternatives.note: Fan-out decides WHAT is in the feed; ranking decides the order. The hybrid answer needs both.
Fan-out-on-read plus an aggressive cache is the pull-side answer, and it is right for low-follower accounts.

components.title: Message Ordering
components.what: Guaranteeing that messages sharing a key are processed in the order they were produced — usually by binding a key to one partition.
reachFor: State transitions must apply in sequence — edits, balances, status changes
The prompt says messages in a conversation or a stream must not appear out of order
A later event invalidates an earlier one and applying them backwards corrupts state
avoid: Operations are commutative; ordering costs parallelism you did not need to spend
Global ordering across all keys is the requirement — that serialises everything
costs: Per-key ordering means per-key serialisation, capping parallelism at the partition count
A partition's throughput becomes the ceiling for its hottest key
Rebalancing consumers has to preserve the guarantee, which complicates scaling
failureModes: Retrying a failed message out of band and applying it after its successor
Repartitioning silently breaking the key-to-partition binding that provided the order
Clock-based ordering across producers giving an order that never actually happened

alternatives.note: If you cannot order, make the operations mergeable instead — CRDTs and version vectors.
Sequence numbers plus idempotent apply lets a consumer detect and discard out-of-order replays.

components.title: At-Least-Once Delivery
components.what: The default durable-messaging guarantee: a message is redelivered until acknowledged, so it may arrive more than once but never zero times.
reachFor: Losing a message is unacceptable and duplicates are survivable
Consumers can be made idempotent
The prompt involves deliveries, notifications or webhooks that must not be dropped
avoid: Side effects are irreversible and cannot be deduplicated — charging a card twice is not a rounding error
Duplicate suppression cannot be implemented anywhere in the pipeline
costs: Every consumer must carry deduplication or idempotency logic
Retry policy is a real design surface: interval, ceiling, jitter, give-up
Duplicate rate is invisible unless you measure it
failureModes: Consumer acknowledges before the work is durable and the message is lost anyway
Retry storm after a downstream outage, amplifying load exactly when it is weakest
Poison message consuming the entire retry budget forever with no dead-letter path

alternatives.note: Effectively-once via idempotency keys and transactional sinks — more machinery, stronger promise.
The required companion: somewhere for a message that has failed enough times to go.

components.title: Exactly-Once (Effectively-Once)
components.what: Making duplicate delivery invisible in the result, by pairing at-least-once transport with idempotent or transactional application.
reachFor: The prompt counts money, inventory or billable events where a double-apply is a real defect
Aggregates must be exact rather than approximately right
You control the sink well enough to commit offset and effect together
avoid: The sink is a third party you cannot make transactional
Approximate results are acceptable — you are buying an expensive guarantee for nothing
costs: Deduplication state per key, which must be kept for at least the retry window
Transactional writes are slower and constrain which sinks you may use
It is only exactly-once within the boundary you control; the edges remain at-least-once
failureModes: Dedup window expiring before a delayed retry arrives, admitting the duplicate you designed against
Dedup store and sink not committed atomically, so a crash between them re-applies
Believing the broker's exactly-once flag covers your external side effects — it does not

alternatives.note: Usually the cheaper route: make the operation safe to repeat and stop trying to prevent repeats.
If duplicates are harmless, do not pay for this.

components.title: Dead-Letter Queue
components.what: A side channel for messages that have failed processing too many times, so one bad item cannot block the pipeline forever.
reachFor: Any at-least-once pipeline — this is the companion, not an optional extra
Failures may be permanent (malformed input) as well as transient
You need to inspect and replay failures after fixing a bug
avoid: Nothing — but it is misused when it becomes a place messages go to be forgotten
costs: Another queue to monitor, and an alerting policy for it
A replay tool, or the DLQ is just a landfill
Ordering guarantees are broken for anything that detours through it
failureModes: Nobody watches it, so silent data loss looks exactly like success
Replaying without fixing the cause, so items round-trip forever
Filling up because the retry threshold was tuned for a transient failure mode that turned permanent

alternatives.note: The delivery guarantee that makes a DLQ necessary in the first place.
Retry policy decides how long something struggles before it is dead-lettered.

components.title: Transactional Outbox / CDC
components.what: Writing the event into the same database transaction as the state change, then shipping it from the table or the write-ahead log — so the event and the data cannot disagree.
reachFor: A state change must reliably produce an event and you cannot afford to lose either
The prompt has a dual-write problem: database plus queue, with no distributed transaction available
Downstream systems (search index, cache, analytics) must converge on the database's truth
avoid: The event does not need to be as durable as the write; a direct publish is far less machinery
You do not own the database, or cannot run a relay next to it
costs: An outbox table plus a relay process, or a CDC pipeline to operate
Additional write volume and a table that needs pruning
Events carry database shape, so the schema becomes an external contract
failureModes: Relay lag making 'reliable' events arbitrarily late
Outbox table growing without bound because pruning was never built
CDC replaying from an old log position and re-emitting a flood of duplicates

alternatives.note: Direct publish when losing the occasional event is genuinely acceptable.
For multi-service workflows, the outbox is how each step reliably announces it happened.

components.title: Stream Processing
components.what: Continuous computation over an unbounded event stream — windowed aggregation, enrichment and joins applied as data arrives.
reachFor: The prompt needs near-real-time aggregates over a firehose
Storing every raw event to query later is too expensive or too slow
Results must update continuously rather than on a schedule
avoid: A nightly batch would satisfy the requirement — batch is dramatically simpler to operate and reason about
The computation needs arbitrary access to all historical data at once
costs: Windowing, watermarks and late-data policy are decisions you cannot avoid making
Stateful operators need checkpointed state, which is the hard operational part
Reprocessing history means replaying the stream, and that has to be designed for
failureModes: Late events arriving after their window closed and being silently dropped
Unbounded state growth in a keyed operator with no TTL
Checkpoint failures forcing a restart that re-emits already-published results

alternatives.note: If you only need counters, a pre-aggregated store may be enough without a stream framework.
Store the points and let the query engine aggregate, when freshness requirements are looser.

components.title: Pre-Aggregation & Rollups
components.what: Maintaining counters and summaries as data arrives, so a read is a lookup instead of a scan.
reachFor: The prompt asks for counts, totals or top-N over volumes too large to scan per request
The same aggregate is read far more often than the underlying events change
Dashboards or leaderboards need sub-second reads
avoid: Query dimensions are unknown or ad-hoc; you cannot pre-aggregate every combination
Exact answers over arbitrary time ranges are required and the rollup granularity would not support them
costs: Every new dimension multiplies the number of aggregates to maintain
Backfilling a new aggregate means reprocessing history
Aggregates can drift from the source and need periodic reconciliation
failureModes: Double counting on retry, so the counter is wrong and nothing signals it
Hot counter — one popular entity's increments exceed a single partition's write throughput
Rollup granularity chosen too coarse to answer a question the product later asks

alternatives.note: When aggregation needs windows, joins or late-data handling, you want a real stream engine.
Sharded counters are the standard fix once one aggregate becomes a write hotspot.

components.title: CQRS / Read-Model Projection
components.what: Serving reads from a second model derived from the write model, so the shape that accepts and validates a change is not the shape that answers a query.
reachFor: The write shape and the read shape genuinely disagree — writes are single-entity and validated, reads are wide joins or fan-ins across many entities
Reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude and the read query is the expensive one
The same underlying facts must be answered in several different shapes, and one schema cannot be optimal for all of them
The write side must stay append-only or auditable, so current state has to be a derived view rather than the record
avoid: One normalized model already serves both sides — the split buys a second store and a pipeline and nothing else
The read must reflect the write immediately; a projection is eventually consistent by construction
Read volume is low enough that an index, a cache or a read replica closes the gap
costs: Two models to keep correct, and a pipeline between them that is now on the critical path for freshness
Every new read shape is another projection to build, backfill and operate
Replay tooling is not optional — a projection you cannot rebuild is a second source of truth you did not mean to create
failureModes: Projection lag surfacing as a user writing something and not seeing it, with no error anywhere
A projection bug silently corrupting the read model while the write log stays correct — invisible until someone reconciles
Read-your-writes broken for the author of a change, because the UI reads the projection it just raced
The two models drifting after a partial replay, so which one is right becomes an operational question

alternatives.note: A read replica scales read VOLUME against the same schema; CQRS is for when the read SHAPE is the problem.
A cache stores the answer to a query you already run; a projection maintains a model no query would produce cheaply.
Rollups are the narrow case — a projection whose read model is counters. Reach for the general form only when the view is richer than that.
This is how the projection is fed: the write commits its change event in the same transaction, and the read model follows the log.

components.title: Idempotency
components.what: Making a repeated operation produce the same result as one execution, usually via a client-supplied key recorded with the effect.
reachFor: Any retry path exists — and in a distributed system one always does
The prompt involves payments, orders, or anything a user could double-submit
Network timeouts leave the caller genuinely unable to tell whether the write happened
avoid: The operation is naturally idempotent already (a PUT of a full resource); adding keys is ceremony
There is nowhere durable to record the key at the moment of the effect
costs: A key store with a retention window, and that window is a real correctness parameter
The key must be recorded atomically with the effect, which constrains your storage choices
Clients must generate and reuse keys correctly — a contract you have to document and police
failureModes: Key recorded after the effect, so a crash between them admits a duplicate
Retention expiring before the last legitimate retry arrives
Client regenerating a new key per retry, which defeats the entire mechanism
Same key reused for a genuinely different request, silently returning the wrong prior result

alternatives.note: The pipeline-level version of the same goal; idempotency is the per-operation building block.
When the operation must hold a scarce resource rather than just be safe to repeat.

components.title: Saga
components.what: A multi-step workflow across services where each step has a compensating action, because no distributed transaction is available.
reachFor: A business operation spans several services that each own their own data
The prompt needs all-or-nothing semantics across boundaries where 2PC is not viable
Steps involve external parties — payment processors, shipping, third-party APIs
avoid: All the state lives in one database — use a transaction and stop inventing
Steps genuinely cannot be compensated (an email is sent, a drug is dispensed) and the design pretends they can
costs: Every forward step needs a compensating step, roughly doubling the logic
Intermediate states are visible to users, so the product must define what they see
Orchestration state has to be durable and recoverable, which is another service
failureModes: Compensation itself failing, leaving the workflow stuck in a half-applied state
Non-compensatable side effect performed before a step that can still fail
Orchestrator crash mid-saga with no durable record of how far it got
Concurrent sagas on the same entity interleaving into a state neither expected

alternatives.note: A two-phase reserve-then-confirm is a lighter pattern when the risk is only about holding scarce stock.
The reliable way for each saga step to announce completion without a dual-write.

components.title: Reservation / Hold
components.what: Temporarily claiming a scarce resource with an expiry, so a user can complete a multi-step flow without it being sold underneath them.
reachFor: Inventory is finite and the purchase flow takes more than one request — seats, rooms, drivers
Overselling is unacceptable but locking for the whole session is unacceptable too
The prompt describes a checkout, booking or matching flow
avoid: The resource is effectively unlimited; a hold is pure overhead
The flow is a single atomic request — just do the transaction
costs: Expiry handling: something must reliably release abandoned holds
Held-but-unsold inventory is real lost revenue during high demand
Users see 'available' counts that include or exclude holds, and you must decide which
failureModes: Holds never expiring because the sweeper failed, silently freezing inventory
Race between expiry and confirmation, releasing something that was just purchased
Hold count not enforced atomically, so concurrent requests both succeed and oversell

alternatives.note: A lock blocks others outright; a reservation is a lock with an owner, an expiry and a business meaning.
When the hold spans several services, the reservation becomes one step of a saga.

components.title: Conflict Resolution
components.what: Deciding what the truth is when two writers modified the same thing concurrently — last-write-wins, version vectors, OT or CRDTs.
reachFor: Writes can happen in multiple places at once — offline clients, multi-region, collaborative editing
The prompt says users edit the same document or record simultaneously
You chose availability over coordination and now must handle the consequence
avoid: A single leader orders all writes — you do not have conflicts to resolve
Silent data loss is unacceptable and you are reaching for last-write-wins because it is easy
costs: Version metadata per item, which can rival the data in size
CRDTs constrain the operations you may offer; OT requires a central sequencer
Some conflicts are genuinely a product decision and must be surfaced to a human
failureModes: Last-write-wins discarding a concurrent update with no trace it existed
Clock skew making 'last' the wrong write entirely
Tombstone and version metadata growing without bound
Merge semantics that are technically correct but produce nonsense the user did not intend

alternatives.note: Route all writes for one key through one partition and the conflict never arises.
Prevent concurrent modification instead of reconciling it — at the cost of availability.

components.title: Leader Election
components.what: Picking exactly one node to perform a role, with an agreed way to notice failure and pick again.
reachFor: Exactly one process must do a job — a scheduler, a compactor, a partition owner
The prompt needs automatic failover without an operator
Multiple nodes doing the work concurrently would be incorrect, not just wasteful
avoid: The work is safely parallel — election adds a coordination dependency for nothing
You would be implementing consensus yourself; use etcd, ZooKeeper or Raft
costs: A consensus system in your dependency graph, with its own availability story
Failover is not instant; there is a detection window where nobody is leader
Leases and fencing tokens must be honoured by the work itself, not just the election
failureModes: Split brain — a paused leader wakes up still believing it holds the role
Election storms flapping the role between nodes under load
Work performed after the lease expired because the worker never checked
The leader becoming a throughput bottleneck nobody planned for

alternatives.note: A lock with a lease is election for one task rather than for a standing role.
Partition ownership by hash gives every node a role without a single leader.

components.title: Distributed Lock
components.what: A lease held in a shared store that grants one holder the right to act on a resource for a bounded time.
reachFor: A critical section spans processes and double execution would corrupt state
A cheap mutual exclusion is needed for a short operation
You need to serialise access to something that has no transaction of its own
avoid: The operation could be made idempotent instead — that is almost always the better answer
The lock would be held across a long or user-driven operation
You are using it as a correctness guarantee without fencing tokens
costs: Every acquisition is a network round trip on the critical path
TTL choice is a genuine tradeoff: too short breaks long work, too long stalls after a crash
The lock store becomes a hard dependency and a bottleneck
failureModes: Holder pauses (GC, VM freeze) past its TTL while still believing it holds the lock
No fencing token, so a stale holder's write is accepted after the lock moved on
Deadlock or livelock from multiple locks acquired in inconsistent order
Lock-store failover losing lock state entirely and admitting two holders

alternatives.note: Make the double execution harmless instead of preventing it. Fewer moving parts, no TTL to tune.
Serialise by routing to one partition owner rather than by contending on a lock.

components.title: Rate Limiting
components.what: Capping how many requests a caller may make in a window, to protect capacity and enforce fairness.
reachFor: A public API where one caller could consume everyone's capacity
The prompt mentions abuse, scraping, brute force or tiered plans
You call a third party with its own quota you must not exceed
avoid: The bottleneck is internal and unbounded work, not caller volume — that is load shedding or backpressure
Legitimate bursts are normal and a hard cap would break the product
costs: Distributed counters mean either shared state on the hot path or approximate limits
Limit values are a product decision that will be wrong at first
Every rejected request still costs you the work of rejecting it
failureModes: Fixed-window boundary allowing double the limit across the boundary instant
Limiter store outage forcing a fail-open (unprotected) or fail-closed (outage) choice you never made explicitly
Limiting by IP and blocking an entire NAT'd office or mobile carrier
No Retry-After, so well-behaved clients retry immediately and amplify the overload

alternatives.note: Rate limiting protects you from callers; backpressure tells callers to slow down because you are full.
When you must drop work by priority under overload rather than by per-caller quota.

components.title: Backpressure
components.what: Letting a saturated consumer slow its producer, so queues stay bounded instead of absorbing an overload until something breaks.
reachFor: Producer and consumer rates can diverge for sustained periods
The prompt has a pipeline where an unbounded buffer would just relocate the failure
Memory or queue depth is a real constraint
avoid: Bursts are short and a buffer genuinely absorbs them
The producer physically cannot slow down — a firehose of external events — in which case you must shed instead
costs: Slowness propagates upstream by design, so the effect is visible to callers
Every stage needs a bounded buffer and a policy for what happens when it is full
Harder to reason about: a slow leaf can stall the root
failureModes: Unbounded queue chosen 'temporarily', converting a latency problem into an out-of-memory crash
Backpressure propagating all the way to a user-facing request path and timing everyone out
Deadlock when two stages apply backpressure to each other in a cycle

alternatives.note: When you cannot slow the producer, drop work deliberately by priority.
A durable queue absorbs bursts; pair with backpressure so 'burst' cannot silently become 'forever'.

components.title: Circuit Breaker
components.what: Tripping a dependency call to fail fast after repeated failures, then probing periodically to see whether it has recovered.
reachFor: A downstream dependency can fail or slow down and you must not go down with it
The prompt asks how the system degrades when one service is unavailable
Retries against a failing dependency would make its recovery harder
avoid: The dependency is genuinely required and there is no meaningful fallback — failing fast just fails faster
Failures are per-request and independent rather than indicative of dependency health
costs: Thresholds and probe intervals are tuning parameters with no obviously right value
A fallback path that is rarely exercised is a fallback path that does not work
State is usually per-process, so behaviour differs across the fleet
failureModes: Tripping on a transient blip and cutting off a healthy dependency
Half-open probes stampeding a recovering service and re-tripping it immediately
Breaker around a non-critical call taking down the critical path because the fallback was never tested

alternatives.note: Retries handle transient failures; a breaker handles sustained ones. You need both, in that order.
Isolate the resources a bad dependency can consume instead of detecting it after the fact.

components.title: Retry with Backoff & Jitter
components.what: Re-attempting a failed call on an exponentially increasing, randomised delay, so transient failures heal without synchronising the fleet.
reachFor: Failures are transient — a timeout, a brief unavailability, a throttled response
The operation is idempotent or has been made so
The prompt asks how you handle partial failure in a distributed call graph
avoid: The failure is deterministic; retrying a malformed request just multiplies it
The operation is not idempotent and duplicates would be harmful
You are retrying at several layers at once, multiplying attempts geometrically
costs: Retries consume capacity at exactly the moment capacity is scarce
Latency budget must accommodate the retries or the caller times out anyway
Attempt caps and total deadlines are required, and are extra parameters to get right
failureModes: No jitter, so every client retries in lockstep and produces a synchronised thundering herd
Retry amplification across layers turning one user request into dozens of backend calls
Retrying a request that actually succeeded but whose response was lost, without an idempotency key

alternatives.note: Once failures are sustained rather than transient, stop retrying and trip.
Move the work off the request path and let the queue own durable retry.

components.title: Load Shedding
components.what: Deliberately dropping or degrading lower-priority work under overload so the system serves its most important traffic instead of failing at everything.
reachFor: Demand can exceed capacity and you cannot slow the source
Some traffic is genuinely more important than the rest — checkout over recommendations
The prompt asks what happens at 10× expected load
avoid: All traffic is equally critical, so there is nothing to shed that does not hurt equally
Capacity is the actual answer and shedding is being used to avoid provisioning
costs: You need a priority classification for traffic, which is a product decision
Shed requests are visible failures, so the client experience must be designed
Detecting overload accurately is harder than it looks — queue depth beats CPU
failureModes: Shedding triggered too late, once queues are already deep and latency is unrecoverable
Shedding cheap requests while expensive ones sail through, so it does not reduce load
Clients retrying shed requests immediately, converting a shed into an amplification

alternatives.note: Per-caller fairness before overload; shedding is the emergency response after.
If the producer CAN be slowed, do that instead — no work is lost.

components.title: Bulkhead Isolation
components.what: Partitioning resources — thread pools, connections, even fleets — so one dependency or tenant cannot consume everything.
reachFor: One slow dependency currently exhausts a shared pool and takes down unrelated paths
The prompt is multi-tenant and one customer must not be able to starve the others
Critical and non-critical work share infrastructure today
avoid: There is only one dependency and one class of work — partitioning buys nothing
Utilisation matters more than isolation; reserved partitions sit idle by design
costs: Lower average utilisation, since capacity is reserved rather than pooled
More pools to size and monitor, each with its own saturation behaviour
Cell-based isolation multiplies deployment and operational surface
failureModes: Pools sized by guesswork, so one saturates constantly while another idles
A shared resource one level down (a connection pool, a database) undoing the isolation above it
Noisy-neighbour effects surviving because the partition was logical, not physical

alternatives.note: Detect and cut off a bad dependency rather than pre-partitioning for it.
Per-tenant quotas achieve fairness without reserving capacity per tenant.

components.title: Inverted Index / Search
components.what: A term-to-document mapping built ahead of time, so full-text and faceted queries are lookups rather than scans.
reachFor: Users query by content rather than by key — free text, filters, facets
The prompt needs relevance ordering, not just matching
A LIKE '%…%' over the primary store would be a full scan
avoid: Lookups are always by primary key
The index would need to be transactionally consistent with the database
The corpus is small enough to filter in memory
costs: A second copy of the data with its own ingestion pipeline and lag
Analysis choices — tokenising, stemming, language — are baked in at index time
Reindexing after a mapping change is a full rebuild, not a migration
failureModes: Index drifting from the source of truth with no reconciliation job to catch it
Deep pagination degrading badly because every shard must return the full prefix
Hot shard from an uneven document distribution
Ingestion lag making just-written content unfindable exactly when users look for it

alternatives.note: For prefix matching specifically, a trie is far cheaper than a general search engine.
When the match should be semantic rather than lexical.

components.title: Vector Search
components.what: Approximate nearest-neighbour lookup over embeddings, retrieving by semantic similarity instead of by keyword.
reachFor: The prompt needs 'find things like this' where the match is meaning, not spelling
Retrieval feeds an LLM (RAG) or a recommender
Users phrase queries differently from the source documents
avoid: Exact matching and filtering are what users need — keyword search is cheaper and explainable
The corpus changes constantly and index rebuilds cannot keep up
You cannot explain why a result was returned and the product requires that
costs: Embeddings must be generated and regenerated whenever the model changes
ANN indexes are memory-hungry and trade recall for latency by construction
Hybrid ranking with keyword search is usually necessary, so you run both
failureModes: Model version drift making old and new embeddings incomparable in the same index
Recall silently degrading as index parameters are tuned for latency
Chunking strategy destroying the context that made a passage meaningful
No metadata filtering, so results are semantically close but structurally invalid

alternatives.note: Lexical search when exactness, filters and explainability matter more than semantics.
Retrieval gets candidates; ranking decides the order. Vector search is the first stage, not the whole answer.

components.title: Ranking
components.what: Ordering a candidate set by a score — recency, affinity, engagement, relevance — usually as a cheap retrieval stage followed by an expensive scoring stage.
reachFor: There are far more matching items than can be shown, and order is the product
The prompt mentions feeds, recommendations, search results or 'what the user sees first'
Simple chronological ordering demonstrably under-serves users
avoid: Chronological is the expected contract and reordering would violate user trust
The candidate set is small enough that order barely matters
You cannot measure whether the ranking is working
costs: A feature pipeline, and features are the expensive, high-maintenance part
Scoring latency forces a multi-stage architecture: cheap retrieval, expensive rank on the top-K
Training and serving must agree, or you get skew that is very hard to debug
failureModes: Training/serving skew from features computed differently in the two paths
Feedback loops where the ranker promotes what it already promoted
Cold start for new users and new items with no signal to rank on
Score computed over a stale candidate set, ranking items that no longer exist

alternatives.note: The infrastructure ranking depends on — where the signals come from at request time.
Precomputed counters make a serviceable ranking signal without a model.

components.title: Geospatial Index
components.what: Mapping 2-D coordinates onto a 1-D key that preserves locality — geohash, quadtree or S2 — so 'what is near me' becomes a range scan.
reachFor: The prompt asks for nearby drivers, restaurants, stores or users
Location updates are frequent and proximity queries must be fast
A naive distance calculation over every row would be a full scan
avoid: Locations are static and few
Queries are by region name or administrative boundary rather than by radius
Exact distance ordering matters more than fast candidate retrieval
costs: Precision level is a tradeoff between cell size and the number of cells to scan
Boundary handling requires querying neighbouring cells, not just the containing one
High-frequency location updates are a write-heavy workload of their own
failureModes: Edge cases at cell boundaries missing a genuinely nearby result
Dense urban cells holding orders of magnitude more entities than rural ones
Fixed precision performing badly in both dense and sparse regions simultaneously
Write amplification from updating the index on every location ping

alternatives.note: Geo cells make a natural partition key, but they inherit population skew — plan for it.
Popular areas are queried repeatedly; a short-TTL cache absorbs most of the read load.

components.title: Bloom Filter
components.what: A compact probabilistic set that answers 'definitely not present' or 'probably present', trading exactness for tiny memory.
reachFor: You need to avoid an expensive lookup for keys that are usually absent
Memory is the constraint and false positives are cheap to recover from
The prompt has dedup or membership checks over a huge keyspace
avoid: A false positive would be a correctness bug rather than a wasted lookup
You need deletion — standard bloom filters cannot remove elements
The set is small enough for an exact structure
costs: Sizing must be decided up front from expected cardinality and target error rate
It degrades as it fills, and the only fix is to rebuild
Another structure to keep in sync with the real data
failureModes: Filter saturating past its design cardinality so the false-positive rate silently climbs
Treating 'probably present' as 'present' and skipping the confirming lookup
Attempting deletion by clearing bits and corrupting other members

alternatives.note: When you need certainty, an exact content-address index is the honest answer.
A negative cache stores known-absent keys exactly, at higher memory cost.

components.title: Trie / Autocomplete
components.what: A prefix tree with top-K completions precomputed at each node, so a keystroke returns suggestions in a single traversal.
reachFor: The prompt is typeahead, search suggestions or command completion
Latency budget is tens of milliseconds because it fires on every keystroke
The suggestion set changes far more slowly than it is queried
avoid: Matching should be fuzzy or semantic rather than prefix-based
The suggestion set is tiny — a filter over an array is simpler
Suggestions must be personalised per user at full precision
costs: Memory grows with the vocabulary, and storing top-K at every node multiplies it
Rebuilds are batch jobs, so new terms appear on a delay
Sharding a trie by prefix creates uneven partitions by construction
failureModes: Popular prefixes ('a', 'th') becoming hot shards that serve most of the traffic
Stale top-K after a spike in popularity for a term the last rebuild missed
Memory blowup from storing full strings at every node instead of references
No typo tolerance, so a single mistyped character returns nothing

alternatives.note: A general search engine with an edge-ngram analyser, when you want fuzziness and are willing to pay for it.
Popular prefixes dominate the distribution; caching their results absorbs most requests before the trie.

components.title: WebSockets / Persistent Connections
components.what: A long-lived bidirectional connection, so the server can push without the client asking and latency is one hop rather than one poll interval.
reachFor: The server must initiate — chat messages, live location, presence, collaborative edits
Updates are frequent enough that polling would be wasteful or too slow
The prompt says real time and means sub-second
avoid: Updates are one-way server-to-client and infrequent — SSE is simpler and survives proxies better
Clients are mobile and frequently backgrounded, where connections die constantly
Update frequency is low enough that polling is honestly fine
costs: Connection state pins users to servers, which breaks stateless load balancing
Memory and file descriptors per connection cap how many fit on a box
You must build reconnect, resume and missed-message backfill yourself
failureModes: Reconnect storm after a deploy or network blip, all clients at once
Messages sent while disconnected being lost with no replay path
Idle proxies and load balancers silently killing connections without a heartbeat
Uneven connection distribution because balancing happened at connect time and never again

alternatives.note: Server-to-client only, over plain HTTP, with automatic browser reconnect. Usually enough for feeds and notifications.
When the recipient is a server rather than a browser, push to their endpoint instead of holding a socket.

components.title: Server-Sent Events
components.what: A one-way stream of events over a normal HTTP response, with browser-native reconnect and event ids for resumption.
reachFor: Updates flow server-to-client only — notifications, progress, token streaming
You want push without owning reconnect logic
Corporate proxies and infrastructure that dislike WebSocket upgrades are in play
avoid: The client needs to send frequently on the same channel — that is WebSockets
You need binary frames
Very high per-client message rates where framing overhead matters
costs: Still one held connection per client, with the same fan-out and capacity implications
Text-only, so binary payloads must be encoded
Older HTTP/1.1 clients hit per-domain connection limits
failureModes: Buffering proxies holding events until the buffer fills, destroying the latency benefit
Missing Last-Event-ID handling, so a reconnect silently loses everything sent while away
No heartbeat, so a dead connection looks identical to an idle one

alternatives.note: When the client must talk back on the same channel at the same cadence.
For infrequent updates, polling a cursor endpoint is simpler than any push channel.

components.title: REST
components.what: Resource-oriented HTTP with standard verbs, status codes and cacheable GETs — the default public API shape.
reachFor: A public API consumed by clients you do not control
You want HTTP caching, proxies and tooling to work without special support
Broad accessibility matters more than payload efficiency
avoid: Chatty internal service-to-service calls where serialisation overhead dominates
Clients need wildly different subsets of the same data and you are drowning in endpoint variants
costs: Over- and under-fetching, which drives clients to make several round trips
Versioning is a real design burden once you have external consumers
No schema enforcement unless you add one
failureModes: Non-idempotent POST retried after a timeout, creating a duplicate resource
Offset pagination degrading and skipping rows as the underlying data shifts
Breaking changes shipped without a version, discovered by customers
Endpoint proliferation as each client gets its own bespoke variant

alternatives.note: Internal, high-volume, strongly-typed service calls where efficiency and contracts matter.
When clients need very different shapes of the same graph and round trips are the pain.

components.title: gRPC
components.what: Binary RPC over HTTP/2 with an IDL-defined contract, code generation, streaming and multiplexing.
reachFor: Internal service-to-service calls at high volume
You want a generated, type-checked contract across several languages
Bidirectional or server streaming is needed without hand-rolling it
avoid: Browsers are first-class clients — it needs a proxy layer to work there
Third-party developers must integrate quickly with curl and a doc page
Human-debuggable payloads matter more than efficiency
costs: Toolchain and codegen in every language you ship
Binary payloads are hard to inspect on the wire
Load balancing HTTP/2 needs L7 awareness; naive L4 pins all calls to one connection
failureModes: Long-lived HTTP/2 connections defeating L4 balancing and hot-spotting one backend
Proto field reuse or renumbering silently corrupting decoded messages
Deadline not propagated, so a cancelled call keeps running downstream
Streaming RPCs leaking when neither side closes

alternatives.note: External consumers, browser clients, or when 'works with curl' is a requirement.
If the caller does not need a response, an event is looser coupling than an RPC.

components.title: GraphQL
components.what: A single endpoint where the client declares exactly which fields of a graph it wants, in one round trip.
reachFor: Many client types need very different subsets of the same data
Mobile round trips are the bottleneck and over-fetching is measurable
The data is genuinely a graph and clients traverse it differently
avoid: One client with stable needs — you have added a query planner for nothing
HTTP caching is important; a POSTed query defeats it
You cannot control or budget what clients ask for
costs: N+1 resolution unless you build dataloader-style batching
Query cost analysis is required or a single query can take down the backend
Caching moves from HTTP into your application
failureModes: Deeply nested query exhausting the server, effectively a self-inflicted denial of service
N+1 database calls hidden behind innocuous-looking field resolvers
Schema growing into a shared dumping ground nobody can deprecate anything from
Errors returned with HTTP 200, so infrastructure-level monitoring reports everything as fine

alternatives.note: Fewer moving parts, real HTTP caching, and usually enough.
When the callers are services rather than varied UI clients.

components.title: Webhooks
components.what: Pushing events to a URL the customer registered, so their server learns about changes without polling yours.
reachFor: External systems must react to your events promptly
Polling would be wasteful at your customer count
The prompt describes integrations, payment events or third-party notifications
avoid: The receiver cannot host a public endpoint
Ordering across events is required — delivery order cannot be guaranteed
Sub-second latency matters; delivery is best-effort with retries
costs: You now own delivery: retries, backoff, dead-lettering and a replay tool
Receiver endpoints are unreliable and slow, and that becomes your operational problem
Signing, secret rotation and replay protection are required, not optional
failureModes: A dead endpoint accumulating an unbounded retry backlog that starves healthy deliveries
Retry storms hammering a receiver that is already struggling
Duplicate delivery corrupting receiver state because no idempotency key was sent
SSRF via customer-supplied URLs pointed at internal addresses

alternatives.note: A polled cursor feed is far less machinery when near-real-time is not required.
The delivery guarantee webhooks provide — receivers must be idempotent.

components.title: Cursor Pagination
components.what: Returning a page plus an opaque cursor pointing at the last item, so the next page seeks rather than counting from the start.
reachFor: Result sets are large and clients page through them
New items arrive while a client is paging — a feed, a log, a timeline
Deep pages must stay as fast as shallow ones
avoid: Users must jump to an arbitrary page number, which cursors cannot express
The result set is small and bounded
There is no stable, unique sort key to build a cursor from
costs: Requires a stable total ordering, usually a compound key including a tiebreaker
No total count without a separate query
Cursor encoding becomes a compatibility surface once clients persist them
failureModes: OFFSET used instead, so page 500 scans and discards 10,000 rows
Items skipped or repeated when new rows arrive between requests
Non-unique sort key causing rows at a boundary to be dropped
Cursor format changed and previously issued cursors stop decoding

alternatives.note: For ranked or faceted results, the engine's own paging semantics apply and deep paging is its own problem.
If the client wants everything new as it happens, push beats repeated paging.

components.title: Transcoding Pipeline
components.what: Converting uploaded media into the ladder of formats, resolutions and bitrates that clients actually stream.
reachFor: Users upload video or audio in arbitrary formats
Playback must adapt to device capability and network conditions
The prompt mentions streaming, adaptive bitrate or thumbnails
avoid: Media is already in a single known format every client supports
Volume is low enough that an off-the-shelf managed service is obviously right
costs: CPU or GPU capacity that dwarfs the rest of the system
Storage multiplies by the number of renditions you generate
Latency between upload and availability is now a product decision
failureModes: Queue backing up during an upload spike, so publish latency grows without bound
A single enormous file monopolising workers and starving everything behind it
Partial ladder published, so some clients get a resolution that does not exist
Retrying a half-finished job and paying full cost again with no checkpointing

alternatives.note: Segmenting first makes transcoding parallel and restartable per segment.
Transcoding makes the renditions; the CDN is what makes serving them affordable.

components.title: Feature Store / Serving
components.what: Serving the same computed signals to training and to inference, with an offline store for history and an online store for low-latency reads.
reachFor: Models need per-entity features at request time within a few milliseconds
The same feature definition must be used in training and serving
Several models or teams share features and are currently recomputing them separately
avoid: One model with features computable from the request payload alone
You have no training/serving skew problem yet and are pre-building for one
costs: Two stores to keep consistent — offline history and online serving
Point-in-time correctness for training data is genuinely hard to get right
Feature definitions become shared contracts with versioning and deprecation
failureModes: Training/serving skew from the same feature computed two different ways
Label leakage from features that encode information unavailable at prediction time
Stale online features silently degrading model quality with no error anywhere
Backfill of a new feature being far more expensive than anyone estimated

alternatives.note: A plain cache of precomputed features when there is one consumer and no training-parity requirement.
Where real-time features are computed before they are stored and served.

components.title: Resource Scheduling
components.what: Allocating scarce, expensive compute — GPUs, batch slots — across competing requests by priority, batching and queueing.
reachFor: The bottleneck resource is expensive enough that utilisation is the design goal
Requests vary in priority or in cost and cannot be treated identically
Batching several requests together materially improves throughput
avoid: Capacity is cheap and elastic — just autoscale
Requests are uniform and a plain queue suffices
costs: Batching trades per-request latency for throughput, and that curve must be chosen deliberately
Priority classes need admission control or the top class starves everyone else
The scheduler becomes a critical, stateful component of its own
failureModes: Head-of-line blocking from one very large request occupying the resource
Batch window tuned for throughput, blowing the latency budget for interactive traffic
Fragmentation leaving capacity unusable because no waiting request fits it
Preemption losing partially completed work with no checkpoint

alternatives.note: When requests are uniform and fair FIFO ordering is acceptable.
Capping demand per caller is simpler than scheduling it, when fairness is the actual goal.

components.title: Audit Log & Provenance
components.what: An append-only record of what was decided and what it was shown, pinned to the versions in effect, so the decision can be reconstructed later.
reachFor: A decision has to be defended to someone external — a regulator, an auditor, a counterparty — months or years after it was made
The inputs came from somewhere you do not control and will not replay: a third-party API, a vendor feed, a model
Money moved, or access was granted or refused, so 'what did we do and on what basis' is a question that will eventually be asked
avoid: The decision is trivially re-derivable from durable inputs you already retain — then the log stores no information you did not have
You only want debugging visibility, where tracing and structured logs are cheaper and are built for the job
costs: The record outlives the schema that wrote it, so it must be self-describing and denormalized rather than a web of foreign keys
Retention is measured in years and is usually a legal floor rather than a tuning knob
Evidence has to be captured at decision time, which means storing the third-party response rather than the query that produced it
