Write amplification on every step of every decision, which is the price of the record being complete rather than sampled
failureModes: Recording the conclusion but not what was shown, so the log asserts a decision it cannot evidence
Pinning the code version but not the policy, prompt or data snapshot — any one of them changing changes the answer
A log the application can update in place, which records the current story rather than what happened
Citing a live source instead of a stored snapshot, so the citation resolves to whatever that source says today
Promising deterministic replay of a non-deterministic process; preserved inputs and a comparison is what you can honestly offer

alternatives.note: Captures every state change for downstream consumers; an audit log captures the decision and its justification, which a change feed does not carry.
When the question is aggregate behaviour over time rather than the defensibility of one specific decision.

components.title: Agent Decision Record
components.what: The row an autonomous decision writes about itself: what it chose, why, how sure it was, and what it was looking at when it chose.
reachFor: A model or agent disposes of work on its own and somebody will later ask why that specific one went the way it did
You need to move the automated share upward safely, which requires measuring where the agent and a human disagree
The decision changes as models, prompts, policy or thresholds change, and you need to attribute a shift to whichever one moved
avoid: The decision is a pure function of stored inputs and a rule you version anyway, where re-running the rule is cheaper and more honest than a narration of it
Nobody ever asks about an individual outcome, only about the aggregate, where offline evaluation over a labelled set answers it more cheaply
costs: A reason enum has to be closed and versioned to stay queryable, which means someone owns a vocabulary that will keep changing
Confidence is worthless until it is calibrated against sampled outcomes per model and prompt version, so the record only pays off alongside a sampling program
A row per decision on the hot path, carrying a rationale and a trajectory reference, so the write is far from free
Recording the threshold in force at the time means the row duplicates config on purpose, which reads as denormalization until the day it is the only answer
failureModes: Free-form reason strings instead of a closed enum, which yields thousands of near-duplicates and no dimension to group by
Storing only the applied outcome, so whether a human agreed with the agent cannot be reconstructed and the autonomy metric does not exist
Treating a self-reported rationale as proof of reasoning rather than evidence of it, when the model narrates after the fact and can narrate wrongly
Collapsing confidence in the answer and completeness of the evidence into one score, which hides the dangerous quadrant where the agent is sure and underinformed
Encoding abstention as low confidence plus an escalation, so missing evidence and conflicting sources land in the same bucket and neither gets fixed
Referencing a threshold that lives only in config, so the row cannot say what bar it actually cleared

alternatives.note: The general provenance record for any decision; this is the shape it takes when the decider is a model, adding calibrated confidence, an abstention state and the agree/disagree column.
The mechanism that raises the automated share; this record is the evidence it runs on, because you cannot widen the band without knowing where the agent and the reviewer diverged.

components.title: Cost Metering
components.what: Attributing the marginal cost of a request to the tenant and unit of work that caused it, then bounding it before it is spent.
reachFor: The per-request cost is large enough that it, rather than CPU or storage, is the first ceiling you will hit
The system decides for itself how much work to do, so it is spending money autonomously and needs a bound rather than a dashboard
You bill by consumption, or you need unit economics per tenant to know whether the product works
avoid: Marginal cost per request is a rounding error next to fixed infrastructure, where this is accounting overhead on the hot path
A flat rate already caps exposure, in which case a budget adds a failure mode without removing one
costs: Attribution has to be threaded through every call path, and one unattributed path is the one that will surprise you
A budget is a new way to fail: you must decide whether exceeding it degrades, queues, or rejects, and say so
Vendor prices change underneath you, so the cost model needs its own update path or it silently stops being true
failureModes: Metering after the fact, which reports the overspend rather than preventing it
Budgeting per request while the expensive unit is a whole session or a whole case, so the cap never binds
A shared pool with no per-tenant cap, where one tenant's batch consumes the month
Counting only the model or vendor bill and missing the retries, which is where a bad day actually gets expensive

alternatives.note: Bounds request volume; a budget bounds spend, and one expensive request can blow the budget while staying inside the rate limit.
Allocates scarce compute between competing work; metering decides what that work was allowed to cost in the first place.
Drops work to protect latency; a budget stops work to protect the bill, and they can disagree about which request to drop.

components.title: Progressive Rollout
components.what: Earning a change's blast radius in stages, so each widening is justified by evidence the previous stage produced.
reachFor: The change alters a decision rather than an implementation, so correctness cannot be established by a test suite alone
Being wrong is expensive or irreversible, and you would rather find out on 1% than on everyone
You need labelled evidence that the change is good, and the earlier stages generate exactly that data
avoid: The change is trivially reversible and cheap to get wrong, where staging is ceremony that slows the loop
You cannot measure the outcome at a slice, since a rollout you cannot evaluate is just a slower deploy
costs: Two code paths live simultaneously, and the shadow path costs real compute while producing nothing a user sees
Comparison infrastructure is the actual work: without a diff between old and new outcomes, the stages tell you nothing
Someone has to own the decision to widen, or a rollout parks at 5% indefinitely and becomes permanent complexity
failureModes: Advancing on elapsed time rather than on evidence, which is a scheduled deploy wearing a rollout's clothes
A slice that is not representative — internal users, one region, the cheapest traffic — so the signal never resembles production
No ratchet back: widening is automated and narrowing is a manual scramble during the incident
Shadow output that is never compared, which pays the full cost of the mechanism for none of the benefit

alternatives.note: Reacts to a failure that is already happening; a rollout bounds how much traffic could have been exposed to it.
Contains blast radius by partitioning resources rather than by limiting how much traffic sees the change.

components.title: Tenant Isolation
components.what: Keeping one customer's data and load away from another's, enforced below application code so a forgotten predicate cannot leak.
reachFor: One deployment serves customers who must never see each other's data, and the boundary is a contractual promise rather than a preference
A single tenant can generate enough load to degrade everyone else, so fairness needs enforcing rather than assuming
An auditor will ask how isolation is guaranteed, and 'every query filters correctly' is not an answer that survives the question
avoid: A single-tenant deployment per customer, where the isolation is the deployment and adding a second mechanism adds only cost
Data that is genuinely global — a catalogue, a public price list — where scoping it invents a boundary that does not exist
costs: Enforcement in the database means every policy predicate needs an index, and a missing one degrades quietly rather than loudly
Per-tenant queues and quotas multiply the things you operate and the things that can be misconfigured
The largest customers often demand physical separation anyway, so you end up operating both models
failureModes: Isolation enforced only in application code, where one query written without the filter is a breach and nothing catches it
Background jobs and admin paths running with elevated credentials that bypass the enforcement entirely — the likeliest real leak
A shared cache keyed without the tenant, so the boundary holds in the database and fails one layer above it
Fairness measured in requests when the expensive thing is work per request, so a quota that looks fair is not
No test that actually attempts a cross-tenant read, leaving isolation a claim rather than a verified control

alternatives.note: Isolates load between workload classes; tenancy adds a data boundary that a bulkhead says nothing about.
Caps a tenant's request rate, which is the load half of isolation and none of the data half.
Splitting by tenant makes isolation physical, at the cost of per-tenant operations and rebalancing.
